title: Despised and cleansed (section 16)
hookLine: if someone is scorned for keeping this teaching, past wrongs are wiped away

cards: The eye-roll lands before the sentence is even finished. Someone at the table mentions they've started sitting quietly every morning, or reading an old sutra on the train, and a cousin snorts. It's small.
It stings anyway. Section sixteen of the Diamond Sutra looks straight at that sting. It doesn't promise that keeping this teaching will make you admired.
It says the opposite might happen, and then says something surprising about what the scorn does.

teach.b: First, the scorn. A good man or a good woman might receive this sutra, keep it, read it, recite it, the Buddha tells Subhuti, and be despised by others for it. Second, the reason.
That person, the sutra says, carries wrongs from former lives, deeds heavy enough to lead to a painful rebirth.
But because they are scorned in this life, those past wrongs are wiped away, and they will reach awakening. The scorn isn't a punishment piling on; it's an old debt settled in a lighter coin.
That's the sutra's way of reading karma: deeds ripen, and sometimes they ripen small. Third, the comparison.
Before he met the earlier Buddha Dipankara, the Buddha says, he served and honored a vast number of buddhas, missing none.

Even so, that merit doesn't come close to the merit of someone in a later age who keeps and recites this sutra. Fourth, the limit. If he told the whole of that merit, some who heard would be bewildered and doubt it.
The meaning of this sutra is beyond thought, and so is its fruit. Notice what the section doesn't say.
It doesn't say scorn is good, or that anyone should seek it out, or that people who mock are villains. It says a slight, borne quietly by someone keeping the teaching, can do a kind of washing.
That's very different from shrugging off harm. A sideways look at dinner is one thing. Cruelty is another, and nothing here asks anyone to stay inside it.

how: Mahayana teachers sometimes read section 16 as a way to meet ridicule with patience: the slight is understood as old karma ripening lightly, borne without retaliation.

o: scorn is good, so it's wise to go looking for it
those who mock the sutra are washed clean of their sins
scorn for keeping the sutra can wipe away past wrongs

games.q: cleansed by scorn: tap the pairs.
p: what may happen, the Buddha says
the earlier Buddha he met long ago
would leave some hearers in doubt

s: section 16 says scorn is good and should be sought out
it never says to seek scorn; it says scorn borne while keeping the teaching wipes away past wrongs.
the Buddha says keeping this sutra outweighs his service to countless buddhas
the merit of his long service doesn't come close, he says.
the Buddha lays out the whole merit in detail
he stops, saying some would be bewildered; the meaning is beyond thought.

games.q: you're keeping the sutra, and someone scorns you for it. what does section 16 say the scorn does?
o: proves you're on the wrong path
wipes away wrongs from former lives
earns you the right to scorn back
games.why: the sutra says past deeds that would have led to painful rebirth are wiped away, and that person will reach awakening.

practice: Bring to mind something you keep that someone once made light of, a habit, a hope, a quiet practice, a faith, and let the remark come back, small and a little sharp.
Instead of a comeback, let the out-breath be the whole reply, and picture yourself carrying on with what you keep, as if the remark had passed like weather.
Keep it to small slights; if something real and painful comes up, set it aside and simply follow the breath.

wordCard.voice: Despised and cleansed. Section sixteen says that when someone keeping this sutra is scorned, past wrongs are wiped away. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: deed, action; section 16 reads scorn as past deeds ripening in a lighter form.

carryVoice: Your line: cleansed by scorn. A small slight can pass like weather. Take care; see you tomorrow.
